extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, librarians, and general readers interested in children's literature and literary awards
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the standards, eligibility rules, selection process, and historical context used to determine the Caldecott Medal and Caldecott Honor Books for children's picture-book illustration. Useful for understanding how candidates are evaluated and how the award has evolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most distinguished illustrations (primary criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Caldecott Medal is an award presented annually to the artist who illustrated the most distinguished children’s picture book in America during the previous year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation centers on the distinction of the illustrations in a picture book published the previous year in America. 'Most distinguished' implies assessment of artistic merit, quality, and contribution to the picture book as a work of children's literature, though the page does not provide a detailed scoring rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: citizenship or residency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The coveted award has been presented to illustrators who are citizens or residents of the United States since 1938.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically limited to U.S. citizens or residents; the article notes some critics proposed expanding eligibility to include authors outside the United States, indicating this requirement is a substantive eligibility rule (and a topic of debate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection by librarian committees
rubrics_metrics.description: The award is presented by the American Library Association and is decided by the Children’s and School Librarians Sections of the ALA (selection by librarians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice to have librarians select winners was intentional to 'eliminate any hint of commercialism' and to encourage literature for children; committees determine winners and may designate Honor Books. Since 1980, separate committees decide Caldecott and Newbery winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of Caldecott Honor Books (runners-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the annual winner, the selection committee frequently nominates up to half a dozen Caldecott Honor Books, recognizing additional noteworthy illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor Books are formal runners-up recognized by the committee; the terminology changed to 'honor books' in 1971. The committee's ability to name multiple honor books is an explicit part of the award process and recognition structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: encourage quality and creative children’s literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The award's purpose was to encourage the creation of quality and creative literature for children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative purpose frames selection: the award is intended to celebrate exceptional artistry and to promote quality in children’s books, not commercial success. It helps explain why librarians (rather than commercial entities) were chosen as selectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical rule on dual-award eligibility (Newbery/Caldecott)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally the rules for the award allowed a book to win only one of the awards (Newbery or Caldecott); that restriction was removed in 1977.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural eligibility rule affected whether a single book could be considered for both writing and illustration awards; its removal in 1977 changed how a work might be judged and honored across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual timing and publication-year scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Caldecott Medal is an annual award honoring the most distinguished children's picture book illustrated in America during the previous year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing constraint: only books published in the prior year are considered. This temporal scope is a substantive part of how candidates are selected (i.e., recent publications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern for diversity and representational equity
rubrics_metrics.description: The award has been historically critiqued for a lack of diversity among its nominees and winners; by the 2020s observers noticed an improvement with people of color making up a more significant number of winners and nominees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not an explicit scoring criterion, diversity and representation have become salient evaluative and policy considerations for the award and its eligibility/selection practices; the article also notes proposals to expand eligibility internationally as part of this conversation.
